newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia surprised by sudden U.S. change in Mir crew.
newsitem.headline: Russia surprised by sudden U.S. change in Mir crew.

text.p: Russian space officials on Thursday said they were surprised by the sudden U.S. decision to replace the next astronaut scheduled to join the troubled Mir space station.
"For us it was very unexpected," said Valery Lyndin, a spokesman for Mission Control outside Moscow.

On Wednesday NASA astronaut Wendy Lawrence appeared at a news conference and expressed her eagerness to fly aboard Mir and replace Michael Foale in September. Then hours after putting her under the international media spotlight, NASA officials announced her backup, David Wolf, would take her place aboard Mir.
Lawrence will still fly on board the U.S. shuttle in mid-September.
U.S. officials said they made the decision because Lawrence, a U.S. Navy pilot, had no experience with spacewalks and did not fit into the Orlan Russian spacesuit.
The next Russian crew abroad Mir will attempt to make vital repairs to the space station, which crashed into a resupply ship on June 25 and is limping along on partial power.
Part of the repairs will require a spacewalk outside the punctured Spektr module, although the NASA astronaut is not expected to participate.

"Because of the number and nature of spacewalks and the nature of spacewalks under consideration by the Russians to repair the Spektr, we have discussed at length the advantage of having another astronaut qualified for these tasks," Frank Culbertson, who oversees NASA's cooperation with Mir, said in a statement on Thursday.
"As a result, the joint decision was made to have all three crew members on board qualified to handle spacewalking tasks," he added.
But there appeared to some some confusion in communications.
Lyndin said Mission Control experts learned of the U.S. decision afterwards. "We only learned about it when our representative who was at NASA called from Washington," he said.
The body of the Russian space suit is the same for all cosmonauts, but the arms and legs are adjustable. Lyndin said smaller Russians had flown in the suit in the past.

"There were no objections to her from our side," he said, referring to Lawrence, who is 1.60 metres (five feet, three inches) tall. "We are only sorry she cannot fly, especially since she was so geared up to do such work."

Russian cosmonauts Anatoly Solovyov and Pavel Vinogradov are expected to blast off for Mir on August 5. On August 20 they will try to reattach Spektr's interior cables, linked to solar panels outside, which should restore most power to the vessel.
They are expected to perform their first spacewalk to inspect the Spektr's external puncture on September 3, and plan to do the repairs after that.

NASA said the launch of the U.S. space shuttle bringing up the next American astronaut may now be delayed to allow Wolf more time to complete spacewalk training outside Moscow. The lift off had been originally scheduled for September 20.
Wolf had been scheduled to join Mir in January.
